translations.text: Discourse of the same holy father of ours, Basil, on faith in the Holy Trinity.
The remembrance of God is always good and insatiable for the God-loving soul, but to set forth the things of God in speech is an act of boldness.
For the mind, through its immeasurable deficiency, falls short of understanding the truth of his works, and speech in turn is unable to express all that has come into the mind.
Now if our mind is so immeasurably unable to reach the height of these matters, and speech is inferior even to our own mind, how is silence not what is fitting?
Otherwise might not the wonder of theology be brought low by the poverty of words?
For the desire for the glory of God is sown by nature in all rational beings, but in speaking worthily of him all alike fall short.
Yet in the desire for piety one person is greater or lesser than another.
But no one is so puffed up and so deluded in mind as to think that he has reached the summit of the inquiry,
but the further he advances toward understanding, the more he recognizes his own weakness.
So it was with Abraham, so it was with Moses, when they were able to see God, as far as it is possible for a human being to see him:
it was then that both of them held themselves in the greatest contempt, for Abraham called himself earth and ashes, and Moses called himself thin-voiced and slow of tongue,
for he saw the weakness of his tongue, that it was unable to speak of the height of the things he had seen.
Yet since every ear is open to hear theology, and the church is never sated with these words, and it confirms the saying of Solomon that:
"The ear shall not be filled with hearing," it is therefore good to speak according to our ability.
And let us speak not of how great God is, but only as far as we can reach.
For even though we cannot see with our eyes the whole of the space that lies between heaven and earth, should we on that account neglect even what we are able to see?
In the same way, let us now show our right belief through these few words, and let us grant to the majesty of his nature the victory over all speech.
For neither the tongues of angels, whatever they may be, nor those of archangels, even if they were to assemble together with the whole of rational nature and speak,
could reach even some small part of his nature, let alone know it completely.
But you, if you wish to speak or to hear about God, leave your flesh, leave the bodily senses, leave the earth,
leave the sea, bring the airs beneath you, pass beyond the seasons, the ordering of the years, the adornments of this earth, and rise above the ether;
pass beyond the stars and their wonders, their beauty and greatness, their workings and their uses,
which bestow on the world their brightness, their order, their course, and how they are joined to and separated from one another.
Pass beyond everything, rise above heaven and become higher than it. With the mind alone gaze about upon the beauties that are there:
the hosts of heaven, the ranks of the angels, the chieftainship of the archangels, the glory of the dominions, the honor of the thrones, the powers and principalities and authorities.
Pass beyond all of these, raise your mind above all creation, and contemplate that all-holy nature:
steadfast, unwavering, unchanging, impassible, simple, unmixed, indivisible;
light unapproachable to the eyes, inexpressible power, uncircumscribed greatness, radiant glory, desirable goodness and kindness,
unimaginable beauty, which powerfully strikes the soul wounded by love of it, but which cannot be revealed in words.
There are the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the uncreated nature, the royal honor, the goodness that is theirs by nature.
The Father is the beginning of all things, the cause of the being of all that exists, the root of the living, from whom came forth the fountain of life, wisdom and power,
the unchanging image of the invisible God, the Son begotten of the Father, the living Word, who is God and is with God, who is and who was.
It is not that he who existed before the ages came in afterward, nor that he was made afterward: he is Son, not created; Creator, not made; builder, not built.
He is everything that the Father is. I have said Son and Father. Keep these for me:
These properties, then, remain in the sonship, and he is everything that the Father is, as the Lord himself said: "All that the Father has is mine."
For truly everything that belongs to the firstborn Son belongs to the image, as the evangelist says:
"We beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father," that is to say,
that the miracles were not given to him by gift and grace, but that by communion of nature the Son has the honor of the Father's divinity.
For receiving is something shared with creatures, but possessing by nature belongs properly to the one begotten.
For as Son he has by nature what is the Father's, and as only-begotten he has everything gathered together in himself, and not one thing is divided off to anyone else.
From the very name of sonship we learn that he shares in the nature, not created by command but proceeding from the Father's essence.
He is with the Father inseparably and timelessly, equal in goodness, equal in power, a sharer of the glory.
And what else could he be but a seal, an image, which shows forth the whole Father in himself?
But whatever words you hear spoken of his human nature, understand that he is ordering the salvation of humankind,
he who appeared to us in the flesh, when he spoke of himself as sent, as able to do nothing of himself, and as receiving a commandment, and when he said:
"My God and your God," and "The Father is greater than I."

So too with being created and made, being sanctified, servitude and obedience, being handed over, learning and receiving a commandment, ignorance, prayer, questioning and being perfected, and things still lowlier than these:
sleep, hunger, weariness, weeping, grief, hiding, or crucifixion and death. For if you wish, it is not difficult to interpret each of all these rightly.
So that you may not go astray, I will tell you briefly, so that you may understand the lofty things as referring to the divinity and to that impassible and incorporeal nature,
and the lowly things as referring to the humanity of him who for our sake became man and became flesh, and was exalted, so that he might exalt us too and teach us understanding,
so that you may know which words are spoken concerning his nature and which concerning the dispensation.
For he who became man was immaterial and incorporeal, and what he was, he remained, and what he was not, he assumed.
From the beginning he was without cause, for what could be the cause of divinity? But afterward he came to be because of a cause, and that cause was our salvation.
He who assumed this coarseness of the flesh was united to the flesh through the mediation of the mind, and he became man and exalted what was lowly, and the two became one,
for the superior prevailed, so that I might become God to the same extent that he became man.
And he was born, but he had also been begotten; he appeared from a woman, but one who was a virgin.
The one is human and the other divine. Here he was without a father, and there he was without a mother. All of this is divine.
He was conceived in the womb, but the prophet, himself still in the womb, recognized him, leaping before the Word for whose sake he had come into being;
he was wrapped in swaddling clothes, but he left behind the wrappings of the tomb and rose; he was laid in a manger, but he was glorified by angels;
and he was made known by a star and worshiped by magi; he fled to Egypt, but he shattered the idols of Egypt;
in the eyes of the Jews he had neither form nor color, but David says, "Comely in beauty beyond the sons of men";
and on the mountain he shone more brightly than the sun, to foreshadow what is to come; he was baptized as a man, but he loosed sins as God and purified the waters;
he was tempted as a man, but he conquered as God, and he commands us not to fear, for he has conquered the world;
he hungered, but he fed thousands, and he is the bread of life and of heaven; he thirsted, but he cried out:
"Let him who thirsts come to me," and he promised to give a spring to believers; he grew weary, but he is the one who gives rest to the weary and the heavy-laden;
he grew heavy with sleep, but he walked lightly upon the sea and rebuked the winds and lifted up Peter as he was sinking; he paid tribute, but from a fish;
and he is King of kings; they called him a Samaritan and demon-possessed, but he saved the man who was going down from Jerusalem and had been handed over to robbers;
and the demons recognized him, and he drowned the legion of evil spirits, and he saw the prince of demons fallen like lightning;
he was stoned, but he was not touched; he prayed, but he hears prayers; he wept, but he put an end to the tears of all;
he asked, "Where is Lazarus?" for he was a man, but he raised Lazarus, for he was God;
he was sold for a slight price, for thirty pieces of silver, but he bought the world at that great price of his own blood;
he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, but he shepherded Israel and now shepherds the whole world;
he was voiceless like a lamb, but he is the Word proclaimed by the voice of the one crying in the wilderness;
He was scourged and wounded, yet he heals every disease and every [?] affliction;
He was nailed to the wood, yet he has turned us back to the tree of life; yet he saved the thief crucified with him and darkened the whole world. He drank vinegar and tasted gall. Who did?
He who turned water into wine, who is the undoer of that evil tasting, who is sweetness and altogether desirable.
He gives up his spirit, yet he has authority to take it up again; and the veil was torn, and the rocks split, and the dead arose.
He died, yet he is life-giving, and he destroyed death by death; he was buried, yet he rose.
He went down to hell, yet he brought up the souls that were there, and he ascended to heaven, and he will come to judge the living and the dead.
And so, let such words as these, which bear the form of lowliness, not give you a pretext for demeaning the divinity of the Only-begotten.
For his humbling of himself toward your weakness is not a diminishing of the honor of his might.
Rather, understand his nature in a manner befitting God, and accept the lowly words on account of his humanity, concerning which,
if we wished to give an interpretation of each one in minute detail, we would bring a great and immeasurable multitude of words into this discourse of ours.
But let us come to the matter before us: that if the mind is able to purify itself of material passions,
and leaves behind even all invisible creatures, and, like a fish from the deep, rises up into purity,
there it will see the Holy Spirit also, where the Son is and where the Father is, who also has all things united in him by nature:
goodness, uprightness, holiness, life. For it is said: "Your good Spirit," and again: "an upright Spirit," and again: "the Holy Spirit."
And the great Paul says: "the law of the Spirit of life."
None of these has been acquired by him, nor has it entered in afterward; but just as heat is inseparable from fire and radiance from light,
so too holiness and life-giving power, goodness and uprightness, are inseparable from the glorious Spirit.
So the Holy Spirit too exists, standing with that blessed nature.

He is not counted among multitudes but is beheld within the Trinity; he is confessed as singular in his individuality; he is not joined to the hosts, but together with the two he completes the Trinity.
For just as the Father is one and the Son is one, so too the Holy Spirit is one.
But as for the other spirits, the ministers of God, in each rank there is a countless multitude.
Therefore do not seek among creatures him who is above creatures; do not bring down the Sanctifier among those being sanctified.
He fills the angels, he fills the archangels, he sanctifies the powers, he gives life to all living beings.
He is spread over all creatures and is present in a different way with each, and nothing is diminished from him by those who receive.
He gives his own grace to all and is not used up upon them; rather, those who receive are full of him, and he remains undiminished.
For the sun shines upon bodies and reaches each one in various ways, and it loses nothing to those who receive it;
so too the Holy Spirit gives his grace to all, and he remains undiminished and undivided; he enlightens all to the understanding of God,
he dwells with the prophets, makes lawgivers wise, perfects priests, strengthens kings, confirms the righteous,
honors virgins, accomplishes the grace of healings, makes the dead alive, looses those who are bound, and makes those who were estranged sons of God.
All this he does through that heavenly birth. If he receives a believing tax collector, he shows him forth as an evangelist; if he dwells with a fisherman, he makes him a theologian;
if he finds a persecutor repentant, he makes him an apostle to the Gentiles, a preacher of the faith, a chosen vessel.
Through this Spirit the weak are strong, the poor become rich, and the unlearned are wiser in words than the wise.
Paul was weak, but by the power of this Spirit his sweat granted healing to the sick.
Peter too had a body of weakness, but by the grace of the Spirit that dwelt in him, the shadow of his body granted healing to the sick.
Peter and John were poor, for they had neither gold nor silver, but they graciously bestowed healing and health, more precious than much gold.
For that lame man had received gold from many and was still a beggar, but when he received grace from Peter, he ceased from begging and leaped like a deer and glorified God.
John did not know the wisdom of this world, but by the power of the Holy Spirit he spoke such words as no fleshly wisdom is able to perceive.
This Spirit is in the heavens and has also filled the earth; he is found everywhere and is nowhere circumscribed.
He is wholly with each one and wholly with God.
He does not dispense gifts as a servant, but apportions graces with authority, for "he apportions to each one as he wills."
He is sent according to the divine dispensation and acts by his own authority.
Let us pray for his indwelling in our souls, and that at no time he may be lacking to us, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,
to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
